summaries.summary: The introduction frames the goal of training AI systems that remain helpful, honest, and harmless even as AI capabilities reach or exceed human-level performance, suggesting new techniques are needed.
Scaling Supervision is defined as techniques that leverage AI to help humans supervise AI more efficiently, enabling the training of systems that behave in desirable ways.
The section argues that an AI assistant that simply refuses all requests would be harmless but useless, motivating the need to balance helpfulness with harmlessness.
The authors note that reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is widely used for training helpful, honest, and harmless AI systems, but they seek simpler and more transparent alternatives.
Constitutional AI (CAI) is introduced as an extreme form of scaling supervision where human supervision is replaced entirely by a set of guiding principles.
The authors demonstrate constitutional methods for training helpful and harmless models from purely helpful RLHF models without any human feedback on harmlessness.
The models used are pretrained language models from prior work, selected to bridge the gap between helpful-only and helpful-and-harmless assistants.
This section evaluates whether language models can correctly identify the most helpful, honest, and harmless response in a conversation to motivate the CAI approach.
The authors describe how to build helpful and harmless models without human feedback labels for harmlessness, starting from a helpful RLHF model trained to follow instructions.
The method involves showing the helpful RLHF model prompts designed to elicit harmful behavior and sampling responses, where prompts come from red teaming experiments.
The training dataset includes 42,496 human-written red teaming prompts and 140,335 additional prompts generated via few-shot prompting.
Model helpfulness and harmlessness are evaluated using Elo scores based on crowdworker preferences in model comparison tests.
The paper examines how the number of principles in the constitution affects harmlessness PM scores, with principles sampled independently at each critique-revision step.
Revisions achieve progressively higher harmlessness scores than initial responses, suggesting that iterative revision improves model behavior.
Critiqued revisions generally outperform direct revisions for smaller models in terms of preference model scores on harmlessness.
The authors investigate whether the critique step is necessary by testing a simplified approach that skips critique and directly instructs the model to generate a revised response.
